title: Elijah Goes First
by: for Elijah, on his sixth birthday

vocab.kidDefinition: bugs that sit up in the trees and buzz all afternoon when it's hot
Kinley's word for seeing a thing one second before it happens
the big rolling sound the sky makes after a flash of lightning
the shape all the tall buildings make against the sky
little bugs that switch their own light on and off in the dark
did a thing over and over until it started to get easier

chapters.title: The Cap on the High Counter

pages.text: Elijah turned six on a Friday, on the hottest day of that whole June. He lived in Atlanta, where summer sits on you like a big warm dog. The city had been waiting on rain that would not come. The sidewalks were hot. The cicadas would not hush.

Elijah was the shortest person in almost every room he walked into, and he had opinions about that. His sister Kinley was nine. Kinley could reach the high shelf. Kinley's braids had beads on the ends that clicked when she turned her head.
For his birthday dinner they went to the burrito place with the blue wall. It had a wood ceiling and cold, cold drinks. And that night, up on the high counter, somebody had left a black baseball cap.

Nobody was wearing it. Nobody was standing near it. It just sat up there like it was waiting on somebody.

Elijah went up on his toes and stretched his arm as far as an arm goes.

He was two whole inches short.

He stretched anyway.

And then, for about half of one second, his feet came off the floor.

The cap came down into his hand. Elijah stood very still, holding it, forgetting to breathe. Nobody came to claim it. So it was his now, on top of everything else he had gotten that day.

Behind him, Kinley's beads had gone completely quiet.

"Do it again," she said.

The alley out back by the dumpsters was not a heroic place, but it was empty. Elijah put the cap on. It sat down over his eyebrows. He bent his knees and jumped. He went up as high as a mailbox and came down laughing.

"I knew," Kinley said. She said it the way you say something you have been carrying around a long while. "I get a longsight. I see a thing about a second before it happens, and my beads go still. Then it happens."

"Since when?" said Elijah.

"Since always. I saw you were going off that porch rail. I saw Daddy drop the eggs." She looked down at her hands. "But seeing a thing doesn't stop it. I never get there in time."

Elijah turned the cap around in his hands and thought about it.

"So you have the longsight," he said. "And I go."

Kinley's beads clicked once.

They practiced all week on small things. A cup going over the edge of the table — Kinley saw, Elijah went. A dog loose on Ponce. A red balloon getting away from a girl outside the market. Small ones. Every single one of them small.

"It's not a whole power," Elijah said on Thursday. "It's half a power."

"So is mine," said Kinley. "Half and half has been a whole thing this entire time, Elijah."

chapters.title: The Night the Lights Went Out

pages.text: On Saturday the rain finally came, and it came all at once. Uncle Manav and Auntie Indira had driven down from New Jersey. Little Azi was with them, small enough to still get carried. They were all on a blanket in Piedmont Park when the sky went the color of a plum.
Thunder walked across the park, slow and enormous. And then the lights of Atlanta went out, block by block. The streetlights. The market. The whole gold skyline, gone like somebody pulling a zipper.

In the dark everybody talked at once. Then Kinley took hold of Elijah's wrist so hard it hurt, and her beads had gone still.

"Azi," she said. "He went after the fireflies. He's down at the pond."

Elijah did not ask her how she knew. He put on the cap. He said the thing they had been practicing all week.

"You see it. I go."

He went up about as high as a porch roof. That is not very high for a superhero. It was exactly high enough.

He found Azi at the edge of the water, both hands full of nothing, looking for a light that had gone out.

Elijah picked him up. Azi held on.

They came down on the blanket. The streetlights came back on all at once. The whole park went gold and dripping.

Auntie Indira said Azi's name about nine times. Daddy sat straight down on the wet grass. Mama got one arm around Elijah and one around Kinley, and did not let go for a while.
Later there was a bath, and dry pajamas, and the good kind of tired. The rain kept going on the roof, soft now, done being loud. Elijah's cap sat on the bedpost where he could see it.

Kinley stopped in his doorway on her way to bed. Her beads clicked twice, quiet.

"Same time tomorrow?" she said.

"Same time tomorrow," said Elijah, who had been six years old for eight whole days.

And the rain kept on, and the dark was warm, and both of them slept.

story_core.notes: Celebration/witnessing spine per doctrine's 'pure celebration' note, structured on pattern §10's evidence logic rather than its self-doubt arc. Elijah's power is real from page 5; the book's work is showing that it is one half of a pair, not a lesser version of Kinley's. Act 3 resolves imperfectly on purpose — 'about as high as a porch roof, which is not very high for a superhero, and was exactly high enough.'

age_fit.notes: Measured, not estimated: 810 words, 20 pages, 3 chapters — inside the 6-8 band (500-900 / 14-22 / 1-3). 97 sentences, average 8.4 words, band target 8-14. Twelve run over 14 and exactly one runs over 20 (the 22-word page-17 line about finding Azi, kept because breaking it breaks the beat). A first pass had 20 sentences over 14 and seven over 20; those were split rather than justified in this note. Kinley is 9/10 and sits above the band — she is written as a character, not as the reader.

personalization.notes: The birthday is the spine, not a dedication line: he turns six on page 1, the cap arrives on his birthday night as the one present nobody bought him, and page 20 closes on 'six years old for eight whole days.' Other callbacks straight off the reference photos and the brief: the black baseball cap on the too-high counter and the burrito place with the blue wall and wood ceiling (photo 1); Kinley's beaded braids, used as the physical tell for her power rather than as decoration (photo 1); being the shortest person in the room, which is the actual six-vs-nine sibling fact; Atlanta heat, cicadas, Ponce, Piedmont Park, the gold skyline. Godparent cameo is load-bearing, not a wave: Azi is who Elijah goes after, so the rescue runs through the real relationship.

craft.notes: Sensory throughout — summer sitting on you like a warm dog, beads clicking and then going still, a wrist grabbed hard enough to hurt, the cap down over the eyebrows. No compliment loops: nobody calls Elijah brave or strong at any point. No teaching voice; the closest thing to a moral is Kinley's 'half and half has been a whole thing this entire time,' which is sibling backtalk, spoken in character. Ends on rain, warm dark, and sleep.

family_tool.notes: parent-guide.md complete with all five required sections. The tool is The Two-Part Power (say what you see / say who goes / name it after), which is a coordination and mutual-witnessing practice for a 6-and-9 sibling pair rather than a regulation tool — honest scoring: it is genuinely usable at 7pm, but it does not do the work a §1 body-based tool does, because this book was not commissioned against a sticky moment.

rubric.pattern_used: authoring-doctrine.md 'When in doubt → buyer wants pure celebration' (witnessing spine, hoped_lesson as spine), structured with story-patterns.md §10's specific-evidence logic
rubric.notes: Sixth-birthday gift book for the author's godson, not a paid Etsy order — authored to the custom-order doctrine anyway. Adaptation: §10 normally runs on a child who says 'I can't'; Elijah never does. The evidence beat is relocated from a mentor's speech to a week of practiced small saves, so the proof is something he did rather than something he was told. Open items for the family, both flagged in the book README: Uncle Manav and Auntie Indira are assumed forms of address, and Mama/Daddy are placeholders for whatever Elijah actually calls his parents.
